quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 RESULTS (call, CFO David Zinsner): fourth quarter revenue was $13.7 billion, 'at the high end of the range we provided in October' - the fifth consecutive quarter of revenue above guidance despite industry-wide supply constraints; AI PC, traditional server and networking revenue were all up double digits sequentially and year-over-year. Non-GAAP gross margin 37.9%, approximately 140 basis points ahead of guidance (higher revenue and lower inventory reserves, partly offset by a higher mix of outsourced client products and the early ramp of Intel 18A for Core Ultra Series 3 / Panther Lake); non-GAAP EPS $0.15 versus $0.08 guidance. Full-year 2025 revenue was $52.9 billion, 'down slightly year-over-year due to constraints across our own manufacturing network and with external suppliers'; full-year non-GAAP gross margin 36.7%; non-GAAP OpEx $16.5 billion, down 15% versus 2024.
quarterly_data.figure: $13.7 billion Q4 revenue; 37.9% non-GAAP gross margin; $0.15 non-GAAP EPS; $52.9 billion full-year revenue

quarterly_data.signal: SEGMENTS: Intel Products Q4 revenue was $12.9 billion, up 2% sequentially, with operating profit of $3.5 billion (27% of revenue), down approximately $200 million QoQ on a higher mix of outsourced products and seasonally higher opex. DCAI revenue was $4.7 billion, up 15% sequentially - 'above expectations and the fastest sequential growth this decade' - reflecting strong demand for traditional server compute; 'Revenue would have been meaningfully higher if we had more supply.' CCG revenue was $8.2 billion, down 4% QoQ even as AI PC units grew 16%.
quarterly_data.figure: DCAI $4.7 billion, up 15% sequentially; Intel Products $12.9 billion; CCG $8.2 billion

quarterly_data.signal: WHY SERVER CPU DEMAND JUMPED: CFO Zinsner said 'all indicators point to the growing and essential role CPUs will play within hyperscale and enterprise AI data centers as inference-driven AI usage expands' - 'The world is shifting from human-prompted requests to persistent and recursive commands driven by computer-to-computer interactions', and the CPU's coordinating role will drive both traditional server refresh and new demand that grows the installed base. Six months earlier every hyperscaler was signaling higher core counts but not higher units; units 'rapidly increased over the third and fourth quarter', and after talking to a few hyperscalers right before the call he 'got the feeling like it was going to be a story we'd feel for several years'. He called the demand 'largely an x86 phenomenon' (an upgrade cycle around older networks that have to talk to AI systems). CEO Lip-Bu Tan said hyperscalers 'are willing to commit long-term agreement', so Intel prioritizes their CPU deployment, and that for hyperscale and high-end OEM/ODM customers 'Their first choice is the CPU from Intel'. Customer feedback points to 'a strong year of growth for DCAI' in 2026, and Intel is partnering with key customers to support their needs beyond 2026.

SERVER ROADMAP RESET: Tan centralized the data center and AI businesses under Kevork to coordinate CPUs, GPUs and platform strategy, and 'made decisive changes to simplify our server road map' - focusing resources on the 16-channel Diamond Rapids and accelerating the introduction of Coral Rapids, with which Intel will 'reintroduce multi-threading back into our data center road map' (customers are asking him to pull it in earlier). Clearwater Forest continues to be supported. Server demand benefits the ongoing Granite Rapids ramp as well as mainstream Sapphire and Emerald Rapids. Intel is also refining a broad AI/accelerated strategy that includes integrating its x86 CPU with fixed-function and programmable accelerator IP, aimed at reasoning models, agentic and physical AI and inference at scale.

CUSTOM ASIC CROSSES A $1B RUN RATE: 'due to the networking demand for the AI infrastructure build-out, our custom ASIC business grew more than 50% in 2025, 26% sequentially and reached an annualized revenue run rate greater than $1 billion in Q4', giving the ASIC team 'a solid base to pursue a $100 billion TAM opportunity'. Tan is 'committing significantly more focused resources and investment dollars' to ASICs (design services, IP building blocks and manufacturing); hyperscalers 'want to build some of the purpose-built silicon with the Xeon CPU included' and are interested in Intel's advanced packaging to make it more complete.
quarterly_data.figure: grew more than 50% in 2025; 26% sequentially; annualized revenue run rate greater than $1 billion; $100 billion TAM

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 GUIDANCE - THE SUPPLY TROUGH: Intel guided Q1 revenue to $11.7 billion to $12.7 billion; the midpoint of $12.2 billion 'reflects a lower end of seasonal Q1', with non-GAAP gross margin of approximately 34.5%, an 11% tax rate and breakeven EPS. Internal supply constraints are 'most acute in Q1': buffer inventory is depleted, finished-goods inventory is 'down to kind of 40% of what it was at peak levels', and the wafer mix shift toward servers that began in Q3 'will not come out of fab until late Q1 '26' - 'it's just literally hand to mouth'. CCG is guided down more than DCAI as internal supply is prioritized to servers; within client Intel is focusing on mid- and high-end parts and pushing any excess into data center. Zinsner said Q1 would be 'well above seasonal' with full supply, expects available supply to improve beginning in Q2 and in each remaining quarter of 2026, and expects better-than-seasonal performance through the year if supply gets there. 2026 OpEx target is $16 billion; the gross-margin goal is to get to 40% first ('34.5% is by no means an acceptable level of gross margins').
quarterly_data.figure: $11.7 billion to $12.7 billion; midpoint of $12.2 billion; approximately 34.5% gross margin; breakeven EPS; finished goods at 40% of what it was at peak levels

quarterly_data.signal: CASH, BALANCE SHEET AND 2026 CAPEX: Q4 operating cash flow was $4.3 billion with gross CapEx of $4 billion and positive adjusted free cash flow of $2.2 billion; 'NVIDIA's $5 billion investment closed in Q4 as expected.' For 2025, cash from operations was $9.7 billion and gross capital investments were $17.7 billion, with capital offsets of approximately $6.5 billion. Intel exited 2025 with $37.4 billion of cash and short-term investments, helped by further Mobileye monetization, the completed Altera stake sale to Silver Lake, accelerated U.S. government funding and investments by the SoftBank Group and NVIDIA; it repaid $3.7 billion of debt and plans to retire all $2.5 billion of 2026 maturities. 2026 CapEx, previously guided down, is now planned at 'a range of flat to down slightly' and weighted to the first half - 'CapEx in 2026 would be to support demand in 2027 and beyond.'
quarterly_data.figure: gross CapEx of $4 billion (Q4); $17.7 billion of gross capital investments (2025); $37.4 billion of cash and short-term investments; NVIDIA's $5 billion investment closed in Q4

quarterly_data.signal: COMPONENT SQUEEZE - DRAM, NAND AND SUBSTRATES: CFO Zinsner said 'over the last several months, industry-wide supply for key components like DRAM, NAND and substrates has come under increasing pressure due to intense demand to support the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure', and rising component pricing, especially relative to the client market, 'could limit our revenue opportunity this year'. CEO Tan called the memory constraint and pricing 'a very big challenge' for the industry: bigger OEM and hyperscale players have more access to memory while smaller ones 'are really challenging to scramble to get the memory', so Intel is allocating CPUs to customers that can complete products ('We don't want to have a CPU, we sent to them, but they are missing the memory'). CFO Zinsner added that for Lunar Lake, Intel was 'relatively aggressive in terms of getting the memory early', though those margins are low because the memory is in package.
